analysis.one_liner: Strips Endangered Species Act protection from the gray wolf nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would have changed the Endangered Species Act to say the gray wolf can never be listed as endangered or threatened anywhere in the United States. That would remove federal protection for the species nationwide, allowing states to manage or kill wolves without the federal review the law normally requires. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and no action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Livestock producers and ranchers in areas with wolves, and hunting interests, would benefit most, since removing endangered-species protection frees states to allow wolf kills without federal oversight. State wildlife agencies would also gain full control over wolf management.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ranchers and hunting interests in wolf country

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a paragraph to Section 4(a) of the Endangered Species Act stating that the Gray Wolf (Canis lupus) 'shall not be treated as an endangered species or threatened species for purposes of this Act,' removing the species from federal protection nationwide. [S3]
Under the Endangered Species Act, a listed species gets federal protection plans and restrictions on harm and killing; removing listing protection returns management entirely to the states. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The gray wolf population, and the public interest in wildlife conservation, would bear the cost: the species would lose the federal safety net that led to its recovery in the first place, including protection in areas where wolves are just beginning to re-establish.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not rely on science: instead of evaluating the wolf's recovery status, it writes a permanent prohibition into the law itself, so the species could never regain protection even if its numbers collapsed. [S3]
A nationwide ban on listing ignores regional variation, removing protection even where wolf populations remain small or are still recovering. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: ranchers and hunters in wolf country gain freedom from federal restrictions on killing wolves. The cost falls broadly on the public, since the bill takes an endangered-species decision out of the hands of wildlife scientists and hard-codes an outcome into law. Its all-or-nothing national design — no state or region could ever protect the wolf under the Act — was its most serious flaw.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Natural Resources Committee from the day it was introduced until Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Chet Edwards introduced the bill on July 30, 2010, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources. [S1] [S5]
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, 9 of 253 House Democrats and 6 of 178 House Republicans. [S4]
No further action was taken; the bill's only recorded action was its referral, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, gray wolves kept their Endangered Species Act protections and the conservation gains of the past decades stayed in place. Ranching and hunting interests hoping to remove federal wolf protection gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Chet Edwards
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently bar Endangered Species Act protection for the gray wolf.

against.name: Nick Rahall
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The small cosponsor group was mixed, 9 Democrats and 6 Republicans, and the bill never advanced far enough for a party-line vote to show.

industries.note: Removing federal protection for wolves lets ranchers and states kill or manage wolves that prey on livestock without federal review. The bill's benefit goes to a narrow set of producers while the species' survival is the public's stake.
Delisting would open wolves to hunting and trapping seasons in more states. This is a benefit concentrated in rural sporting interests, at the cost of protections the broader public has a stake in.
